steps.text: I can change a fraction to a decimal by dividing the top by the bottom.
I can tell if a decimal stops, repeats, or never ends and never repeats.
I can tell if a number is rational or irrational by looking at its decimal.
steps.example: 0.375 and 0.333… are rational; π = 3.14159… is irrational

steps.text: I can name every number group a number belongs to.
I can write a repeating decimal as a fraction.
I can explain why a decimal with a pattern can still be irrational.
steps.example: 0.1010010001… is irrational: no block repeats the same way.

steps.text: I can draw a diagram of the real numbers and explain how the groups fit.
steps.example: Every integer is rational, but no number is both rational and irrational.

steps.text: I can explain why a fraction like 2π/5 can still be irrational.
steps.example: 2π is irrational, so 2π/5 is irrational too.

steps.text: I can square or cube a number.
I can find the square root or cube root of a perfect square or cube.
I can recall perfect squares up to 20² and cubes up to 10³ quickly.
I can tell if a square root is rational or irrational.
steps.example: √40 is irrational: 40 is not a perfect square.

steps.text: I can solve equations like x² = 121 and x³ = −27.
I can use a root to find a side from an area or volume.
steps.example: A cube holds 125 cm³, so each edge is ∛125 = 5 cm

steps.text: I can work out expressions with roots and exponents, one step at a time.
I can explain why x² = 25 has two answers, but x³ = −8 has one.
steps.example: 5² and (−5)² both make 25; a cube keeps the sign, so only (−2)³ = −8.

steps.text: I can trap a square root between two whole numbers.
I can use a calculator to round a square root to the nearest tenth.
I can mark about where a square root or π goes on a number line.
steps.example: √14 ≈ 3.7, a little closer to 4 than to 3

steps.text: I can put rational and irrational numbers in order from least to greatest.
I can estimate a square root to the nearest tenth without a calculator.
I can square a decimal to tell which is bigger, like 7.2 or √52.
I can prove my estimate is right by squaring numbers on each side.
I can order square roots, cube roots, and π together.
I can name the base and exponent, and write a power as multiplication.
I can multiply or divide powers with the same base.
steps.example: m⁸ · m³ = m¹¹ (add); x⁷ ÷ x² = x⁵ (subtract)

steps.text: I can raise a power to a power by multiplying the exponents.
I can find the value of zero and negative exponents.
I can multiply and divide terms with numbers and variables.
I can use several rules in one problem and end with positive exponents.
I can find and fix mistakes in someone else's exponent work.
steps.example: (5³)⁴ is 5¹², not 5⁷ — multiply the exponents, don't add.

steps.text: I can explain why a⁰ = 1 and why a⁻¹ = 1/a.

title: Scientific notation to estimate and compare

steps.text: I can tell if a number is written in scientific notation.
steps.example: 3.8 × 10⁵ is; 38 × 10⁴ is not (38 is too big)

steps.text: I can change scientific notation into a regular number.
I can write a very big or very small number in scientific notation.
I can round a number to one digit times a power of 10.
I can order numbers in scientific notation from smallest to largest.
I can find exactly how many times bigger one number is than another.
I can round two real amounts, then estimate how many times bigger one is.
I can use just the exponents to tell about how many times bigger.
I can multiply numbers in scientific notation.
I can divide numbers in scientific notation.
I can fix an answer so the first number is between 1 and 10.
I can solve a word problem when one number is written the regular way.
I can solve word problems that take two or more steps.
steps.example: 60,000 homes × 200 L a day = 1.2 × 10⁷ L; in 30 days, 3.6 × 10⁸ L

steps.text: I can check if an answer makes sense by estimating with regular numbers.
steps.example: 2,500 cars × 1,000 kg ≈ 2.5 × 10⁶ kg, so 2.5 × 10⁹ kg is too big.

steps.text: I can choose a unit that makes my answer easy to picture.

title: Equations and inequalities in one variable

steps.text: I can solve a two-step equation by undoing each operation.
I can distribute and combine like terms, then solve.
I can solve an equation with x on both sides.
I can solve an equation with fractions and check by plugging in.
I can tell if an equation has one, no, or infinitely many solutions.
I can solve and graph an inequality, flipping the sign when I divide by a negative.
steps.example: −5x ≤ −15 → x ≥ 3: closed dot at 3, shade right

steps.text: I can explain why an equation has no solution or infinitely many.
I can write and solve an equation or inequality for a real situation.
I can check if a point makes both equations true.
steps.example: (2, −1) in y = −2x + 3 and y = x − 3: both give −1 ✓

steps.text: I can solve a system by graphing and finding where the lines cross.
steps.example: y = ½x + 1 and y = −2x + 6 cross at (2, 2)

steps.text: I can use slopes and y-intercepts to tell how many solutions a system has.
steps.example: y = 4x − 1 and y = 4x + 6: same slope → no solution

steps.text: I can solve a simple system just by looking at it.
I can solve a system by substitution.
I can write a system of equations for a word problem.
I can solve a word-problem system and say what the answer means.
I can explain no solution or infinitely many using the graphs.
steps.example: Same slope, different y-intercepts → parallel lines never cross → no solution.
